# Combat

Negotiations fail. Deals go south. Somebody decides what you’re carrying is worth more than your life. When that happens, the city doesn’t slow down to let you think it over, and every choice you made before weapons were drawn starts paying out.

Combat in Shadows is fast and expensive. A fight that would eat a whole session elsewhere resolves here in twenty minutes, because the system is built to keep moving and because people who take bullets stop fighting back. There is no long middle where you trade blows until somebody’s numbers run out. Once the bullets start flying, every second after becomes a question of what you’re willing to lose.

No matter who is involved, every combat encounter has the same general shape:

1.  **The GM frames the space.** Who’s in the room, what's between you, what's dark, what's already on fire, and everything else to describe the setting.

2.  **Determine Order of Engagement.** Everyone makes a Combat Sense check to determine the Order of Engagement. Ties are rerolled until turn order is clear.

3.  **Take turns.** Each person or side acts in order. When everyone's had a chance to act, the round ends.

4.  **Reset.** The round closes out.

5.  **Repeat** until the stakes resolve or the situation turns into something else.

## The Setting

Shadows isn’t played on a grid, so position is described, not measured. There's no flanking, no facing, and no bonus for standing behind somebody — what the space gives you is cover, darkness, and distance. The GM will describe elevation, obstacles, and other interesting features that can give an edge to you or your opponents. Each of the elements can make it more difficult to reach your targets.

### Cover

Only a fool stands in the open when engaged in a firefight. Cover encompasses the range of objects you can put between yourself and your enemies, with each reducing the chance that they’ll be able to reach you, or vice versa. Only the best cover counts, and cover does not stack.

- **No Cover** refers to those who stand in the open, exposed from every angle.

  - Attackers have **no penalty** to attack targets with No Cover.

- **Partial Cover** refers to anything that covers around half of your body, like crates, a doorframe, or a car door.

  - Attackers take a **-1 Penalty** to attacks against targets with Partial Cover.

- **Heavy Cover** includes those larger objects where only your head and weapon are visible — a firing slit, an engine block, or a corner you peek around.

  - Attackers take a -**3 Penalty** to attacks against targets with Heavy Cover.

- **Full Cover** means you’re completely obscured and there is no line of sight to you. That doesn’t mean you’re completely protected, as explosions don’t need to see you in order to hurt you.

  - Targets with Full Cover can only be attacked indirectly, through weapons, powers, or spells that have an area of effect and don’t require line of sight.

### Visibility

NYTE City is full of dark places where sunlight and neon give way to deep shadows and gloom. Visibility encompasses the range of light in any situation, impacting the ability to see and hit your targets. The darker the room, the easier it is to use **Stealth** to set up a **Surprise** or **Ambush**.

- **Bright** refers to areas with ample natural or artificial light that do not impede visibility in any way.

  - Attackers have no penalty to attack targets in Bright areas

- **Dim** refers to areas with poor lighting, flickering neon or half-lit warehouses that make it difficult to determine distance, shape, or color.

  - Attackers take a **-1 Penalty** to attacks against targets in **Dim** areas

  - Stealth checks get a +1 bonus

- **Dark** refers to moonlit alleyways, the tunnels of the Underground, or a warehouse floor on backup power bathed in dark red light.

  - Attackers take a **-3 Penalty** to attacks against targets in **Dark** areas

  - Stealth checks get a +3 bonus

- **Blind** means the area is so choked with smoke, the lights are completely out, or a flashbang just went off in your face. Either way, you’re attacking a memory, not a target. See Conditions and Recovery for more information regarding the Blinded condition.

  - Attackers take a **-5 Penalty** to attacks against targets in **Blind** areas

  - Stealth checks get a +5 bonus

### Distance

Every weapon has a range at which they are most effective, and while you can technically shoot someone while standing at arm’s length, it’s quite difficult to hit someone with a grenade at 400m. With weapons, range is not measured meter by meter, but rather in bands of effectiveness. Attacking under your range is fine, but attacking one level outside of your range significantly reduces your chance to hit, granting a **-3 penalty** to attackers. Attacking two levels outside of the range is ineffective.

- **Close (0-3m)** is someone within arm’s reach or in the same room. Melee and Martial Arts weapons fall under Close range, though some have Reach.

- **Short** (3-40m) is someone at the far end of the room or across the street. Close enough to hit without getting any of it on you. Handguns, Shotguns, and Grenades dominate this space.

- **Medium (40-120m)** is the gang down the block or across the yard. You’ll want to steady yourself before taking wild shots. SMGs and Rifles have no issue if you’ve got discipline.

- **Long** (120-400m) is the sweet spot where only the talented and well-funded pick their targets. Rifles and Heavy weapons make a difference here.

- **Extreme** (400m+) is reserved for those Sniper rifles, vehicle weapons, satellite-based lasers and other things not likely in your hands.

#### Thrown Weapons

Thrown weapons don’t have a range, you do. This is good to know before you start littering the street with throwing knives or wasting good grenades that might explode before ever getting close to the target.

| BOD  | Reach       | Range  |
|------|-------------|--------|
| 1-3  | ~15 meters  | Short  |
| 4-7  | ~ 30 meters | Short  |
| 8-10 | ~60 meters  | Medium |
| 11+  | 120m+       | Long   |

You can always throw short. What you can’t do is throw less than the blast radius and expect to come out unscathed.

> **Callout: Stacking the Space**
>
> Cover, visibility, and distance answer at once, and they combine to ruin your shot — but only so far.
>
> You killed the power on the block, so the buildings are running on reserve. The electronic lock cycles to its default unlocked position and you slip inside. The garage is lit dull amber — enough to show you where the vehicles are, not what's behind them. Movement at the far end. Then a SMARTbrace flares for half a second behind a forklift, sixty meters of parked cars between you, and you have your target.
>
> You also have a problem, and you built most of it yourself.
>
> The amber-lit room is **Dark**, which is **−3**. The forklift is **Heavy Cover**, another **−3**. And sixty meters is **Medium** — one band past what a handgun is for, and **−3** again. That's −9 penalty on a shot you haven't taken yet.
>
> **Penalties stop accruing at −8.** That isn't the GM refusing you the shot. It's the situation telling you to change something before you take it, and every number in that stack has an answer.
>
> **\* Close the distance.** Medium becomes Short and the range penalty is gone. Crossing sixty meters of open floor while somebody watches the door is a different problem, but it's a problem you chose.
>
> **\* Change the light.** Goggles, a flare, or somebody finding the working circuit. Dark becomes Dim, and −3 becomes −1.
>
> **\* Change the angle.** Move until the forklift isn't between you and him. Heavy becomes Partial, or nothing at all.
>
> **\* Change the weapon.** The only one of the four you can do without leaving the spot you're standing in.
>
> Take the shot anyway and it's −8 and a prayer. The cap exists so the answer to an impossible shot is a decision instead of a die roll.

### Engagement

As with other encounter types, the Order of Engagement determines who is acting when — whether that is as individuals or as sides, in waves. This is never more important than in combat, when the difference between life and death might be a split second decision.

- To determine Order of Engagement, everyone involved makes a Combat Sense check. Order proceeds in descending order from the highest result.

- In the event of a tie, characters will re-roll until an order is set.

- Exceptions

  - Characters with the Combat Paralysis Disadvantage always go last.

  - Characters may choose to delay their turn until a specific condition is triggered.

  - Characters may attempt to Surprise or Ambush at the start of Engagement

#### Surprise and Ambush

Stealth is how a fight ends before it starts. Catching the other side off guard means they cannot answer properly, and with preparation the first turn decides the rest.

**Resolution:** Surprise and Ambush is determined from a single Opposed Check — Attackers' Stealth against Defenders' Awareness, made during Engagement. If the Stealth fumbles or the Awareness holds, the Engagement proceeds as normal.

**Surprise** — At least one attacker wins the check. The defenders are alerted as it happens, with no time to do anything useful about it.

- Attackers gain +1 to their first Attack roll

- **Surprised** defenders are limited to Fast Actions on their first turn.

- No penalty to defense: being caught out is not the same as being helpless, and a Dodge is reflex rather than planning.

**Ambush** — Every attacker wins. The defenders never saw it coming.

- Attackers gain +3 to their first Attack roll

- **Ambushed** defenders cannot act during the first round

- Ambushed defenders cannot defend, and attacks are resolved against Difficulty 10

**Limits:** Surprise or Ambush is limited to once per encounter. After the first shot everyone knows you are there.

- Weapons with the Silent tag are an exception, so long as Stealth is not broken. A hidden sniper can continue to Ambush if nobody uncovers their position.

#### Delaying an Action

On your turn, you can choose to delay your action until a specific condition is triggered. This is a risk, as it is possible to delay for a condition that is never triggered.

Examples include:

- “I’m going to shoot the first person that opens the door”

- “I’ll hit the detonator once someone walks over the bridge”

- “I’ll toss the EMP if anyone goes for the Combat Rig”

If the condition is met, the character who delayed gets to act immediately. If the condition is not met, the character has missed their opportunity to act. Once that round is at Reset, turn order resumes as before, and the character can chose to act normally or delay based on a condition once their turn comes back around.

## The Toolkit

As with social and environmental encounters, combat has its own rhythm and flow. During combat, the round includes everyone in it, operating at nearly the same time over the course of 15-20 seconds. You take your turn when it comes up on the engagement order, but your crew and your enemies are also taking their turns. The effective crew isn’t the one that hits hardest. It’s the one that coordinates well.

### On Your Turn

Three to five seconds. That sounds like nothing until you watch somebody spend it — come through a doorway, unleash a burst into the man on the other side, and duck behind the crates before he can call for backup. It's long enough to change a room. It isn't long enough to change your mind twice.

What you do comes out of three pools that don't trade against each other. You move. You take one Fast Action. You take one Standard Action. Spend them in whatever order the moment calls for: shoot and then run, run and then shoot, or shoot while running — it’s your call.

Or you spend the whole turn on a Stunt, which is a different arrangement entirely.

#### Movement

Movement is how you stop being where the shooting is. Your MOB is the baseline, and how hard you push it decides how much of your attention is left for anything else. The penalties are to attacking *while moving*. There’s a difference between running across the room to get a closer shot and strafing across the room while unloading your magazine.

- **Walk — MOB, no penalty.**\
  You're moving and you're still fighting. Weapon up, eyes on the corners and on the man who hasn't committed yet. This is the pace of somebody who intends to shoot on the way, and shooting on the way costs them nothing.

- **Run — MOB ×3, −1 to attacks while moving.**\
  You cover three times the distance, and most of your attention is on where your feet are landing. You can still shoot; you just won't shoot as well. The impact is minor, but it can make a difference against a difficult target.

- **Sprint — MOB ×6, −3 to attacks while moving.**\
  Everything you have is being spent on being somewhere else. Firing while sprinting is more for distraction than lethality, and the die shows it.

Break the movement wherever you want. Out of the doorway, a burst into the man at the console, then the rest of the way to the crates — and you do want to reach the crates.

Dropping to the ground is free. Getting up spends your Move, which is the part worth thinking about before you go down — you can drop and keep shooting, but you can't dive for cover, pop up, and keep moving.

#### Fast Actions

A Fast Action is what the hand that isn't on the trigger does with those three seconds. It's rarely the impressive part of a turn and it's frequently the reason you’re still standing at the end.

- **Reload.** Slide a fresh magazine home, pull a grenade off the bandolier, draw an arrow from the quiver. If you carry more than one kind of ammunition, you can swap types once in a turn — the round you need is never the round already chambered.

- **Administer aid.** A hypo out of your vest and into your own thigh, or into the arm of a crewmate who has stopped arguing about whether they're fine. If you’ve got the Çredits, a Nanomed Kit works the same way and does considerably more.

- **Work an item.** Snap a Silver Card. Thumb the detonator on charges you set an hour ago. Kill the lights and change what everybody in the room is capable of.

- **Trigger a Talisman.** Speak the word or make the contact that lets go of something you prepared days ago. The spell was cast during inscription — there's no Spellcraft roll here, only the release. If it reaches out and touches somebody, a Spell Attack still applies.

- **Make a check that doesn't need your hands.** A Tactics read on how the room is actually arranged or an Occult Lore identification of whatever came through the wall. Forewarned is forearmed, and a bit of information can be the difference between taking a breather and needing a breathing tube once the dust settles.

You get one Fast Action during your turn, not a list. You don't shoot, reload, shoot, reload your way through three seconds, and you don't reload, inject, hit the alarm, and gauge the response time inside the same breath. Three seconds is three seconds, and the crews who decide early what their other hand is doing tend to outlive the crews who decide late.

You get a second Fast Action at Reset, which can make a world of difference to the crew.

#### Standard Actions

The Standard Action is your focus — the thing you were actually doing this turn.

**Attack.** A fist, a blade, a burst, whatever is in your hands. This is most turns for most people, and there's no shame in it. The question is never whether to attack. It's what you're attacking with and from where.

**Combat Maneuver.** An attack that takes control instead of health. You reach for one when the target is worth more alive than dead — somebody who knows a name you need — or when they're worth more on the floor than upright, because a man on his back isn't shooting your crew while you deal with his friends.

**Cast a spell.** The Spellcraft check decides whether it happens at all. If it reaches out and touches somebody in particular, that's an attack roll like any other.

**Activate a Power.** Spending SFR to do what your nature lets you do, up to what your Rate of Use allows. Some Powers are quick enough to be Fast Actions and say so. Changing shape is not one of them.

**Anything that takes all of your attention.** Breaching a door. Working a terminal while the room decides whether to become a problem. Dragging a downed crewmate to the safety of cover.

You get one Standard Action per turn. Some Advantages, Milestones, or Powers may grant an additional **attack** — but that’s firing twice rather than slinging bullets and spells in the same turn.

#### Stunts

On some turns, the ordinary version won't do. You tactically dive across the room while firing at the guard. You slide across the warehouse floor to slip under the shutter at the last second. You go through the window instead of around the building. You take out the guard’s knee at 300m so you can keep him for questioning later.

A Stunt is the whole turn. No movement, no Fast Action, no separate attack — you’re attempting one extraordinary thing instead of doing three ordinary ones — and it doesn’t always work.

**Making one work:**

- **Roll a natural 4 or better on the die, and beat the opposed roll.** Both. A natural 4 that loses isn't a Stunt, and a win on a natural 3 isn't either.

- **Once per round.** Declaring it spends it, whether or not it succeeds.

- **Fall short on the die and it resolves like any other roll.** You don't fail outright — you just don't do anything worth telling stories about. If the total still wins, the attack lands like any other.

**The scale is one cinematic moment, not three:**

- Diving through the window while throwing a grenade behind you and shouting an epic one-liner — yes.

- Diving through the window while throwing a handful of grenades behind you and deploying a glider to soar to the neighboring rooftop while shouting an epic one-liner — that's three turns, and two of them weren't Stunts.

**It’s what you do when nothing else works, not how you get around:**

- Sprinting from behind cover while drawing guns and going full auto at a room of opponents — yes.

- Constantly diving and rolling from cover to cover while spraying bullets the whole time — no.

Improvising is easier than inventing from nothing. Three Stunts come pre-built, one for each firing mode, and each buys something that mode can’t do on its own. Each option costs the entire turn and still requires a natural 4 or better.

### On Your Crew’s Turn

Your turn ends and the fight keeps moving without waiting for you. The runner beside you goes through the door you were both watching, the medic hauls somebody out of the open, and you're still standing in that room while all of it happens. Turns overlap, which means you're never actually idle — you're watching, you're talking, and you're deciding what to do with the one action you get before the order comes back around to you.

Your real contribution to somebody else's turn arrives at Reset. By then you've seen the whole round: who moved, who didn't, and what the room looks like now that four people have rearranged it. You get one Fast Action to answer with. Reloading spends it on yourself and calling the shot spends it on the crew, and only one of those is the reason your crew is a crew.

Six people taking six separate turns are six people having six separate fights in the same building.

#### Free Actions

Some things cost nothing and can happen at any point in the round, including in the middle of somebody else's turn. They're free because they take no real time and produce no mechanical advantage.

- **Say something worth saying.** There's no time for a speech. "Go for the eyes" has won fights. So has "don't!"

- **Drop to the ground.** Getting up again spends your Move, but going down costs nothing at all.

- **Let go of something.** Drop the weapon, release the grip, open your hand and let the case fall.

- **Look.** You always know what you can see from where you're standing.

The limit is fiction rather than economy. Three to five seconds is four words, not four sentences.

#### Coordination

There isn’t explicitly a mechanical value in coordination for you and your crew, no +1 to attacks when going after the same target. The benefit lies in efficiency of your actions. An average fight lasts four rounds, so wasted turn is wasting a quarter of everything you had to offer.

**Tell people what you can see.** Talking is free, and your view of the room is unique to you. The guard on the catwalk is only a surprise to the crew who didn’t look up.

**Spend your Reset on someone else.** Everyone gets a Fast Action during Reset. You could choose to Reload, or you could choose to call out the target, get a read on the room, or hit a crewmate with a life-saving syringe. You brought the crew to the fight for a reason.

**Don’t solve the same problem twice.** If two of you are shooting the same guard, that’s one turn spent on someone who’s going down already. If your crewmate is hacking the mainframe, a second pair of hands on the keyboard won’t make it go any faster. Take out an additional target, hack the cameras, toss a smoke grenade, or anything else that can accomplish multiple goals at once.

**Focused fire saves lives.** That said, the big bad in the corner of the room might take 5 rounds to drop if you spread your ammo around taking down smaller targets, or two turns if you coordinate the assault. It’s much easier to survive two turns than five.

**Know where your people are.** A grenade doesn’t discriminate, and neither does a spray of bullets. Controlled Burst and Controlled Spray exist because someone learned that the hard way.

### On Your Enemy’s Turn

Somebody is trying to kill you, and you're allowed to do something about it.

Defending is free, it's unlimited, and it doesn't get worse with repetition. A character attacked ten times in a round answers ten times at full value, and the tenth answer is as good as the first. Being outnumbered isn't itself a penalty — five attackers taking turns are five separate contests, and you meet each one with everything you have.

What erodes your defense is never how many people are shooting at you. It's Pain, a change in the space around you, or a Condition that limits how you're able to respond.

**Your enemies work from a shorter list than you do.** They don't improvise. Each one has a fixed set of things it does — what it was trained for, what it was built for, or what it has survived long enough to keep doing — and no enemy invents a Stunt in the middle of a fight. Some have a signature move, and those are the dangerous ones. A corporate sniper puts a round into the first person who hasn't reached cover yet, and it does that every time, because that is what it is for. Enemies without a signature move will never surprise you with one.

What that buys you is a fight you can learn. The second time you meet something, you already know what it can do to you.

#### Defensive Actions

**Dodge.** You can attempt to dodge against any attack. You’re getting out of the way of something that was aimed at you, which is why it works equally well against a bullet and a blade. You’re not *actually* dodging bullets, but you’re moving in a way that makes you harder to hit.

- Roll 1d10 + Dodge + Modifiers

**Parry.** You can attempt to parry hand-to-hand attacks (Melee and Martial Arts) only, and only with a hand-to-hand weapon (Melee and Martial Arts). You aren’t avoiding the attack — you’re meeting it in kind and sending it somewhere else.

- Roll 1d10 + Melee + Parry Bonus + Modifiers

**Scramble.** You can attempt to get out of the way of attacks that expand outward from a single point — a grenade, a charge, a spell, etc. Dodging is directional, and a blast doesn’t have a direction. Full Auto is a directional attack and does not fall under this.

- Roll a MOB Essence Check. Unless the attack says otherwise, that's TN 8, TH 2 — the standard for a grenade or a placed charge. Spells and other effects set their own numbers.

- Meeting the Threshold means you got low enough, far enough, or behind enough to avoid the worst of it — the Condition doesn't land. The damage usually still does. What a Scramble buys against any particular attack is listed with that attack, and a few of them let you get away clean.

#### When You Can’t Defend

**Not defending.** The attack resolves against Difficulty 10 instead of against a roll. That covers anyone unaware of you, anyone ambushed, and anyone turning their back on a Reach weapon. Range, cover, and visibility still apply — a target behind an engine block isn't an easy shot simply because they never saw you.

**Helpless.** Paralyzed, Stunned, or Unconscious. Any roll of 2 or better hits, and a natural 1 still botches. Damage resolves normally, because being Helpless doesn't skip the part where somebody has to actually kill you. A Stunned target at full Health Levels who takes a knife is a Stunned target who has been stabbed once.

**Finishing.** When a Helpless target is already out — at zero Health Levels, Unconscious, or Dying — an attacker standing over them decides how it ends, and whether they leave a body or somebody who wakes up later. Unnamed opposition gets no say. Named characters and crewmembers do.

### Reset

The round ends, and none of it happened in the order you read it. You were moving while somebody else was shooting, while a third person was halfway through a door, while a fourth was still holding a grenade with the pin already gone. Turn order is how a fight gets resolved. It isn't how a fight looks.

- **One Fast Action each.** Reload, settle into the cover you reached, take a read on what just happened.

- **Everything that happens once a round happens now.** Bleeding takes its point. Fire keeps burning. Durations run down. Whatever you're trying to shake off gets its check.

Then Engagement comes back around and the next round starts.

Reset is bookkeeping with a pulse. The Fast Action is real — it's why people survive rounds they had no business surviving — but it isn't a second turn. You can be somewhere you already got to. You can't get somewhere new.

## Making an Attack

Every attack in Shadows, from a thrown knife to a full-auto burst, follows the same five steps.

| The rule | At the table |
|----|----|
| **Declare.** Name your target and what you're doing. Firing mode, Combat Maneuver, and Stunt are declared here — before dice, not after. | *"Single shot, the one behind the crates."* Single fire, because at thirty meters the ACC bonus is worth more than volume. |
| **Count the modifiers.** Range band, cover, visibility, your movement, your Pain Level, and whatever your gear and Advantages contribute. | Crates are Partial Cover, −1. The warehouse is Dim, −1. Thirty meters is Short, which is what the Ironside is for, so distance costs nothing. Single fire adds the weapon's ACC, +1. **Net −1.** |
| **Roll the attack.** 1d10 + your Skill + modifiers. | Handguns sits at +14. The die comes up 6. **6 + 14 − 1 = 19.** |
| **The target answers.** The defender may Dodge, or Parry if it's melee and they have something worth parrying with. Both are 1d10 + skill + modifiers. | He Dodges. Die of 8 on a Dodge of +7 is **15**. The crates don't help him here — cover makes you harder to hit, not faster. |
| **Compare and resolve.** Higher total wins. Ties go to the defender. On a hit, damage is dealt and armor answers. | 19 beats 15. The Ironside deals **7**. His vest rolls PROT and turns 3 of it, taking **4 damage** total. |

### Tens and Ones

Shadows is a d10 system, and a few special things happen when rolling.

- **A natural 10 hits.** It doesn't matter what the defender rolled.

- **A natural 1 misses.** It doesn't matter how badly the defender rolled either.

- **Every 10 explodes.** Roll again and add. Each additional 10 keeps the chain alive, and every 10 in the chain lands another hit — a Single becomes two, a Burst becomes four, a bat swing connects twice — until a 10 stops coming.

- **Full Auto works differently**, because it counts differentials rather than hit-or-miss. The exploded die adds to the total as normal, and each 10 adds +1 hit on top.

- **Defenders explode too.** A 10 on a Dodge or Parry rolls again and adds, and keeps going. It does not stop a natural 10 from the attacker. Nothing does.

When exploding, most weapons simply do additional damage. Some weapons, like grenades, may inflict Conditions depending on the number of explosions. These are noted on the weapon itself, where x1 means a single explosion, x3 is three explosions, and so on. The same grenade might start with damage, escalate to Injured, and top out at Maimed.

### Melee and Martial Arts Attacks

The Melee skill covers Melee weapons and Thrown weapons, grenades included. The Martial Arts skill covers Martial Arts weapons and Combat Maneuvers, including strikes, holds, and different Martial Arts styles.

- **Damage is enhanced by BOD**. Weapon damage is indicated as “BOD+3” or “BOD+6” per strike, and is calculated by adding the BOD score to the bonus. A character with BOD 5 using a BOD+3 weapon does 8 damage per strike. That same character using a bareknuckle attack would do only 5 damage per strike.

- **Style matters.** Bladed weapons can inflict Bleeding and may have Armor Penetration (AP). Blunt weapons can inflict Stunned or Disoriented.

- **Parry** requires a handheld weapon. Melee or Martial Arts weapons can Parry, but the Melee skill is used to calculate a Parry attempt. Some weapons have a Parry bonus that further enhances their ability to defend.

#### Reach and Leaving a Fight

Some weapons carry the Reach property, which lets them attack opponents leaving Close range.

- Leaving Close range under your own power gives every Reach-armed enemy in contact a free attack. It is considered a Free Action.

- You cannot defend against a Reach attack, because you are turning your back on the fight and running away. The attacker makes the attack at Difficulty 10, though range, cover, and visibility penalties still apply — which is why people drop smoke grenades before fleeing.

- A successful hit with a Reach weapon causes damage. Other Conditions may apply, depending on the weapon used.

- Forced movement does not trigger a Reach attack, and neither does disengaging from a Stunned opponent.

### Ranged Attacks

Ranged attacks are useful when you want to engage your opponent at a distance – typically Short range and beyond.

- Skills include the Archery skill for bows and crossbows, as well as every firearm skill – handgun, submachine guns (SMG), rifles, heavy weapons, and beam weapons.

- Grenades occupy a unique space because they are technically used at range, but rely on the Melee skill to attack. The distance they can be thrown is limited by the attackers BOD, as seen earlier in the chapter.

- Ranged weapons are most susceptible to penalties based on range, cover, and visibility — you can’t hit what you can’t see.

#### Rate of Fire – Single, Burst, Full Auto

Every ranged weapon has a listed Rate of Fire (RoF) that indicates how much ammunition is being sent downrange at your target per attack.

Each RoF carries different benefits or drawbacks, so it is useful to know what firing mode to use for each situation. Sometimes you need a single well-placed shot, other times you want to spray and pray. Ammunition is spent by mode, and knowing how many you have left in the magazine can be the difference between an awkward mid-fight reload or dropping your opponent.

**Single (S):** Single fire spends 1 round. It isn’t the right answer every time, but when it is there is nothing better.

- **Accuracy:** Add the weapon’s ACC bonus when rolling to attack

- **Damage:** Add the weapon’s Kicker Die when determining damage.

- **Silence:** Single is the only RoF that uses the Silent tag, enabling you to stay in Stealth after firing.

- **Stunt – Called Shot:** This allows Single fire to do increased damage or apply the Injured or Maimed condition.

**Burst (B):** Burst fire spends 3 rounds. It’s likely your go-to, due to the balance between damage and accuracy.

- **Accuracy:** Burst has no attack bonus or penalty. It is one attack roll against one defense roll, and all three shots either hit or miss as a group.

- **Damage:** Damage comes as a damage packet, which can overwhelm armor that would otherwise block a Single shot. Three rounds from a weapon that deals 8 damage per round arrives as a packet of 24 damage against one roll of armor.

- **Stunt – Controlled Burst:** This allows an attacker to spread the 3 rounds across up to 3 targets.

**Full Auto (F):** Full Auto fire spends 10 rounds. This is great for crowd control or where accuracy is less important than damage.

- **Accuracy:** Hits are determined by differential. A Rifle attack roll of 15 against a Dodge roll of 10 results in 5 hits.

- **Damage:** Damage comes as a damage packet, which can overwhelm armor that would otherwise block a Single shot. Up to ten rounds, based on the differential, hitting the armor in one packet.

- **Crowd work:** Full auto can be used as an area attack, hitting a group of targets based on their individual ability to Dodge the attack.

- **Stunt – Controlled Spray:** This allows an attacker to spread up to 10 rounds across up to 10 targets.

### Area Attacks

Some attacks cover ground instead of picking a target. Everyone standing in that ground is involved, including your own people, which is the entire reason area attacks are interesting.

There are two shapes to area attacks, and they resolve differently. A **Blast** goes off in a place, and everyone near it is looking at the same number. A **Spray** comes out of your weapon, and a finite quantity of it gets distributed among whoever was worst at getting clear.

#### Blasts

A blast expands outward from a point of impact — a grenade, a placed charge, an area spell. The damage belongs to the device rather than to your aim or your arm, so it doesn't matter who you were looking at.

- **Declare the zone.** Name where it goes. Everyone and everything inside the radius is in it: allies, enemies, bystanders, and objects.

- **Roll against Difficulty 10.** You're throwing at a place, not a person. Range, cover, and visibility still apply, and a miss means it went somewhere you didn't choose.

- **A blast doesn't need line of sight.** This is the one attack that reaches a target in Full Cover, which is most of why anyone carries one.

- **Everyone inside Scrambles.** A MOB Essence Check each. Objects don't defend.

- **The damage is the same for everybody.** What differs is what the Scramble bought them.

#### Sprays

A spray comes out of the weapon in a cone — full auto, a flame projector, some spells. Rounds are finite, so the question isn't who's in it. It's who was worst at getting out.

- **Declare the zone.** A cone, roughly three meters across at its widest, containing everyone and everything in the way.

- **Roll the attack normally.** SMG, Rifle, Spell Attack, whatever's in your hands.

- **Everyone inside Dodges.** Objects are Difficulty 10.

- **Rounds fill from the worst defense upward.** Each target takes hits equal to the amount you beat them by, starting with whoever rolled lowest, until the rounds run out. Ten rounds is ten rounds however many people were standing there.

- **Stunt: Controlled Spray overrides the order**, if you'd rather choose than let the dice choose.

**A miss is not without consequence.** A botched throw flies off course and finds a building or a grounder instead of a crowd. A spray that misses still hits a backstop, which might be as mundane as a wall or as interesting as a gas main.

### Combat Maneuvers

A Combat Maneuver is an attack that trades damage for control. Declare it before you roll; on a hit you inflict a Condition instead of dealing damage. This can be an alternative if you need to subdue a target for questioning, rather than kill them outright.

| Maneuver | Inflicts | Effect | Recovery |
|----|----|----|----|
| Grapple | Grappled | -5 to anything requiring sophisticated movement | Source removed, or BOD/REF opposed essence against grappler (escapee’s choice) |
| Knockdown | Prone | Movement halved, Attack/Defense at -3 penalty. | Move spent to Stand |
| Disarm | Disarmed | You aren’t holding your weapon and cannot use it. | Recover the weapon, spending Move, Fast, or Standard to do so. |
| Stun | Stunned | Helpless | BOD Essence TN 8 TH 2 |

#### Unarmed Attacks

Unarmed attackers can use the Martial Arts skill to attempt different Combat Maneuvers, with bonuses to each technique based on the style of Martial Arts in which they are trained. For example, training in Commando gives a bonus to Stun, whereas training in Krav Maga gives a bonus to Disarm.

#### Weapon Attacks

Martial Arts weapons carrying the matching Tag — Disarming, Knockdown — can also be used for Combat Maneuvers, imparting damage as well as the desired Condition. Weapons without these tags cannot be used for Combat Maneuvers.

See *Conditions and Recovery* for more information.

**Grappling has a follow-through.** Once you have hold of somebody, moving them is a Martial Arts check at Difficulty 15 — and the attempt hands them a chance to break loose, an opposed BOD or REF Essence against you, their choice of stat. They get that same check at every Reset regardless.

**A disarmed weapon goes where the attacker says it goes.** Recovering the weapon could be quick (Fast Action) if it’s dropped at their feet, or challenging (Fast + Move) if it’s flung across the room.

### Use a Power

Using a Power is a Standard Action, unless otherwise specified. Powers are where certain Archetypes, such as Werewolves and Vampires, really shine on the battlefield.

Characters spend their Spiritual Force Rating (SFR) on either a single-use or continuous-use powers, up to their Rate of use (RoU) per turn.

Powers range in function and can be offensive, defensive, or utilitarian.

See *Archetypes* for more information on specific Powers.

### Cast a Spell

Casting a spell is a Standard Action and resolves in two parts.

1.  **Spellcraft roll**. Determines whether you pull together enough Aether and shape it into the spell you intended. For some spells this is the only step.

2.  **Spell Attack.** Used if the spell interacts with a target, in which case the target has a chance to avoid it — Dodge against an aimed spell, Scramble against an area effect, or a relevant Essence check against anything reaching into the mind or body.

See *Magic* for information on specific spells and their effects.

### Stunts — Called Shot, Controlled Burst, and Controlled Spray

#### Called Shot — Single fire only. 

The Called Shot stunt lets you spend a full turn spent deciding exactly where the round goes. It doesn't make the attack hit harder. It decides what the hit ruins, and how much of the target's armor gets a say.

- **Head — double damage.** No body armor covers a head. Against a target without a helmet nothing intervenes: the damage doubles and goes straight to Health Levels. A helmet resolves the shot as a hit to the torso instead, and body armor applies normally.

- **Limb — normal damage, plus Injured.** Whether their armor has anything to say about it depends on what they bought. With a weapon capable of taking the limb off, Maimed instead.

- **An object — whatever that object does when it's hit.** The fuel line, the transformer, the strut, the cable holding the crate above the room.

Before you spend a turn on it, ask what they're wearing. Looking costs nothing, and a jacket tells you the arms are covered and the legs aren't.

A Called Shot from a handgun spends a turn to roughly match what a burst would have done anyway. A Called Shot from a rifle that only fires single rounds is the entire reason somebody carries one.

#### Controlled Burst — Burst only

A burst normally puts all three rounds into one target. Controlled Burst divides them instead: name up to three targets before you roll, one attack roll, each of them defends separately.

Three rounds into one person arrive as a single packet against one roll of armor. The same three split across three people arrive as three separate hits against three separate rolls, and armor that would have failed against the packet will often stop each of them cold. You're trading damage for reach.

#### Controlled Spray — Full Auto only 

Full auto already spreads, filling from the worst defensive roll upward — which means the dice decide who takes the rounds, and it's frequently the least dangerous person in the room. Controlled Spray is you deciding instead.

Name your targets before you roll, up to ten. Hits land where you called them rather than where the defenses fell. Center mass only — no locations, no multipliers, no headshots.

This is what you use when the person who matters is standing behind two people who don't, or when your own crew is somewhere in that cone.

## Damage and Armor

The contest is settled and somebody lost it. Now it costs them something.

- **Total the damage.** A single attack deals the weapon's damage. Burst and Full Auto deliver a damage packet — every round that landed adds together into one figure.

- **Armor answers.** The defender rolls PROT and adds RES where the damage type allows it, and that total comes off the damage. Armor-piercing skips RES entirely, though PROT still rolls. Enemy armor is static and doesn't roll.

- **What survives both** comes off Health Levels, left to right.

**Armor can stop a hit completely**, and often does. A light round against heavy plate accomplishes nothing except telling the wearer where you are. What you brought to the job decides more of a firefight than how well you shoot.

### Damage Types

Two kinds of damage that don’t behave like the rest — Massive and Withering.

#### Massive Damage 

This is a special kind of damage from a higher class of weapon, including vehicles, siege weapons, and explosives operating outside the envelope of personal combat. Against vehicles, mechs, and fortifications it behaves like any other damage. Against a person it doesn't behave like damage at all.

Massive strips Integrity equal to the weapon's damage and takes 1 Health Level per 10 points of that damage. If the hit drops the armor to 0 — or there was nothing there to begin with — take an additional Health Level.

Those Health Levels are gone rather than emptied. Rest doesn't bring them back and neither does a chem. Somebody has to put you back together properly.

Gear lists which sources deal it.

#### Withering Damage 

Withering damage is unique to supernatural creatures, like Werewolves and Vampires, that have the ability to regenerate. Certain weapons and ammo types are designed to bring down supernatural creatures, primarily by interrupting the regeneration effect.

When attacked by a weapon inflicting withering damage, armor works as it always does. However, any damage beyond what your armor can handle will cause wounds that won’t close on their own.

The only recovery from withering damage is to get away from the source — the silver slug in your chest, the blessed arrowhead in your leg, or the UV light shining down from the sky — and get some rest and medical intervention.

### Wear and Integrity

Armor is consumable, and those who want to live to fight another day understand this at their core. Every fight you’re in takes a toll on the Kevlar and cloth you’ve wrapped yourself in. In most cases your body splits the bill with your gear, and you end up patching holes either way. On rare occasions, the armor is able to stop everything thrown at you – maybe the caliber was small, the angle was off, or you simply used a little Luck.

When that happens, the armor pays a little extra.

- **In the moment.** A hit that armor soaks entirely still costs the armor 1 integrity per attack absorbed. Five people plinking you with Cheapshots will wear even the toughest armor down eventually. The same thing is true on the other end for Massive Damage — if they’re bringing the tank rounds out to drop you, your armor is going to pay the price immediately.

- **After the fight.** Anyone who took a hit, regardless of how much went to the vest or your chest, makes a roll for wear and tear on their armor. The GM determines the scope of the fight and the roll comes off the top of your Integrity: 1d4 to 1d10, depending on the fight.

- At Integrity 0 the armor stops protecting properly. RES is gone until somebody repairs it, and PROT remains, because cracked plate still turns a round now and then, just not when you need it to. Armor driven to 0 by Massive damage isn't repairable. It's scrap.

### What Happens to You

Losing Health Levels changes what you're capable of, and most of what actually takes a character out of a fight is a Condition rather than a number. Pain, the Conditions, the Shock Check, Dying, and everything that can be done about any of it live in *Conditions and Recovery.*

Three things from that chapter matter while you're still in the fight:

- **Pain applies to everything.** Each Pain Level costs you −1 on Skill Checks, one die out of every Essence pool, and 5% off every Breaker Check. It's bounded at 3 and it doesn't care that you were in the middle of something.

- **Conditions mostly clear at Reset**, which is why Reset matters more than it looks like it should.

- **A single hit that takes half your Health Levels** puts you on the floor if you fail the Shock Check, and the floor is where Helpless lives.

## Aftermath

Combat ends when one side is dead, gone, or finished — and in NYTE City, finished is far more common than dead. Almost nobody fights to the last body. Gangers break when the person running the floor goes down. Corporate security withdraws when the contract stops being worth the casualties. Professionals leave the moment the job turns unprofitable, and they remember your face on the way out.

The most useful question in a firefight is rarely whether you can win it. It's what would make them stop, and whether you can afford what they'd want in exchange.

**What the body remembers.** Health Levels come back, eventually. The rest is slower. A crew that wins every fight and ends every month in a clinic is a crew working past its equipment, and the city has a word for people who solve every problem the same way. It isn't a compliment, and it travels.

Your GM remembers who was in the room. Not just who you put down, but who watched you do it and who paid for the cleanup afterward. A reputation for violence is still a reputation — it opens certain doors immediately and welds others shut for good.

## Playing it Out

**Setup:** Torque shook the electrical current off and came around through the vehicle ramp, four minutes behind. The handoff is happening in a loading bay on the service level: a courier with a case, and two people being paid to make sure he leaves with it.

**Players**

- Alex as Torque, Professional (Wheelman)

- Maya as Nyx, Arcanist

**GM:** The bay is lit, but only down the center — the racks on both sides are in shadow. Courier's at the tailgate of a parked grounder about thirty meters out, case in hand. Two others: one behind a stack of pallets near him, one walking the near side of the bay who hasn't seen you yet. Roll **Combat Sense**.

*Nyx 17, Security A 14, Torque 12, Security B 9, Courier 6.*

**Maya:** Nyx first. The courier's the whole reason we're here — I want the case, not the case's friends. Dart at the courier.

**GM:** Spellcraft first. That's whether it comes together at all.

*Maya rolls 5 dice: 9, 8, 4, 10, 2 — three Hits.*

**GM:** It comes together. Now the attack roll, because you're pointing it at a person.

**Maya:** Thirty meters, he's beside the grounder but not behind it.

**GM:** Partial Cover, so you're at −1. Bay's lit down the middle, so no visibility penalty.

*Maya rolls 7 + 11 − 1 = 17. Courier defends with Dodge and rolls 12.*

**GM:** He's got a case in one hand and nowhere useful to be. It catches him in the shoulder — take your Spell Power, that's 6. He drops to one knee and does not drop the case.

**GM:** Security A saw where that came from. She's behind the pallets with a Chatter, and she's not being careful about it — full auto, all ten rounds.

**Maya:** At me?

**GM:** At you. Full auto is −3, and thirty meters is Medium, which is what an SMG is for.

*Security A rolls 6 + 12 − 3 = 15. Maya defends with Dodge and rolls 12.*

**GM:** Full auto counts the difference, not hit-or-miss. She beat you by three, so three rounds find you. That's a packet — 5 damage each, arriving as 15 all at once, and your armor gets one roll against the whole thing.

*Maya rolls PROT: 2, plus RES 3. That’s 5 defended of 15.*

**GM:** 10 gets through. That's two Health Levels, and now you're at Pain Level 1 — everything you roll from here is a point worse.

**Alex:** My turn. I'm coming out of the ramp mouth and putting the grounder between me and the pallets. How far?

**GM:** Twenty meters, and it's a clean floor this time.

**Alex:** MOB 5, so that's a run. I move first, stop behind the grounder, *then* shoot. Single, at the one with the SMG.

**GM:** Good — you stopped, so the run costs you nothing. She's behind pallets, so that's Partial, −1. Single fire gives you the Ironside's ACC, +1.

*Alex rolls 8 + 14 + 1 − 1 = 22. Security A defends with Dodge and rolls 13.*

**GM:** She's reloading and looking at Nyx. The Ironside deals 7, her vest absorbs 2, five gets through — and that's a ballistic hit that opened something. She's **Bleeding**.

**GM:** Security B has spent the round crossing the bay and he's close enough now to be a problem. He isn't shooting you, Torque — he's coming over the hood, and he's trained. **Knockdown**, on Martial Arts.

*Security B rolls 9 + 11 = 20. Alex defends with Dodge and rolls 6 + 13 = 19.*

**GM:** By one. He comes across the grounder and takes your legs out from under you. No damage — a maneuver trades damage for control. You're **Prone**, which means standing up costs your Move next turn.

**GM:** Courier's turn, and the courier is not in this fight. He's up, he's got the case, and he's running for the personnel door at the far end. He's not going to make it this round. He is going to make it next round.

**GM:** Everybody's acted. **Reset.**

**GM:** Security A is Bleeding — that's a point, and she's going to keep losing one every round until somebody stops it. Everyone gets a Fast Action.

**Maya:** I'm settling into the racks. Actual cover this time.

**Alex:** I'm on my back behind a grounder and I can see the door he's running for. I'm using mine to say so — "Door on the north wall, he's forty meters out and he's not stopping."

**GM:** Free, actually. Talking doesn't cost you anything. So you've still got a Fast Action.

**Alex:** Then I reload.

That's one round. Nobody has died, the crew is hurt, one enemy is bleeding, one PC is on the floor, and the man they came for is closer to the door than he was thirty seconds ago.

Recap

- **The room decided more than the dice did.** Nyx's Dart took a −1 because the courier stood beside a grounder rather than behind it. Torque's shot took a −1 for pallets. Neither penalty was large, and both were the difference between a comfortable roll and a nervous one.

- **Moving and then shooting is free. Shooting while moving is not.** Alex ran twenty meters, stopped, and fired at no penalty. Had he fired on the way, that's −1, and against a target already behind cover it starts to matter.

- **Full auto counts the gap, not the hit.** Security A beat Nyx by three and three rounds found her. Her armor answered with 5 — which would have stopped every one of those rounds cold if they'd arrived one at a time. Arriving together as 15, that same 5 stopped a third of the damage packet. The packet is why volume beats precision against armor.

- **A Combat Maneuver dealt no damage and changed the fight anyway.** Torque is Prone, which costs him his Move next turn, which means he isn't chasing the courier. Security B spent his turn making sure of that.

- **The courier is the encounter.** He never attacked anybody. Everything the crew does from here is measured against how close he is to that door, and combat ending is not the same thing as combat being won.

- **Talking is free, and Alex nearly paid for it anyway.** Calling out the door cost nothing, which left him a Fast Action he'd have otherwise spent on four words.

## Quick Reference

**Modifiers** — penalties to the attacker. They add, and they stop at −8.

| Cover            | Visibility | Distance           | Moving    |
|------------------|------------|--------------------|-----------|
| None —           | Bright —   | In band —          | Walk —    |
| Partial −1       | Dim −1     | One band past −3   | Run −1    |
| Heavy −3         | Dark −3    | Two past — no shot | Sprint −3 |
| Full — no shot\* | Blind −5   |                    |           |

*\*Area attacks reach Full Cover. Nothing else does.*

**Range bands**

| Close | Short | Medium  | Long     | Extreme |
|-------|-------|---------|----------|---------|
| 0–3m  | 3–40m | 40–120m | 120–400m | 400m+   |

**Rate of Fire**

| Mode      | Rounds | Roll | Result                                            |
|-----------|--------|------|---------------------------------------------------|
| Single    | 1      | +ACC | Hit or miss. Kicker die. Called Shot available.   |
| Burst     | 3      | flat | All three or none, as one packet.                 |
| Full Auto | 10     | −3   | One hit per point of differential, as one packet. |

**Movement** — break it up freely around your other actions

| Pace   | Distance | Attacking  |
|--------|----------|------------|
| Walk   | MOB      | No penalty |
| Run    | MOB ×3   | −1         |
| Sprint | MOB ×6   | −3         |

**Free Action** — as many as make sense, on anybody's turn

- **Talk** — four words, not four sentences

- **Drop prone** — standing up later costs your Move

- **Let go of something**

- **Look**

**Fast Action** — one on your turn, one at Reset

- **Reload** — fresh magazine, grenade off the belt, arrow from the quiver; swap ammo type once per turn

- **Inject** — battle chem or Nanomed Kit, yourself or somebody in reach

- **Activate an item** — silver card, detonator, lights

- **Quick check** — Tactics, Occult Lore, anything that doesn't need your hands

- **Shout** — four words, not four sentences

**Standard Action** — one per turn

- **Attack** — anything from a fist to a Hammerlock

- **Combat Maneuver** — Martial Arts skill to Grapple, Knockdown, Disarm, Stun

- **Cast a spell** — Spellcraft check, then an attack roll if it's aimed

- **Activate a Power** — SFR, up to your Rate of Use

- **Full-attention work** — breach, hack, drag somebody clear

**Stunt** — once per round, replaces your entire turn

- Natural 4 or better *and* beat the opposed roll

- Fall short on the die and it resolves as an ordinary roll

**Defense** — free, unlimited, no penalty for being outnumbered

| The threat             | The answer                                         |
|------------------------|----------------------------------------------------|
| Aimed at you           | Dodge — REF Skill                                  |
| In reach, hand to hand | Parry — Melee Skill plus the weapon's bonus        |
| Filling the space      | Scramble — MOB Essence, TN 8 TH 2                  |
| In your body           | BOD Essence — poison, current, pressure            |
| In your head           | WILL Essence — fear, compulsion, magical illusions |
| You aren't defending   | Difficulty 10                                      |
| Helpless               | Hit on 2 or better, natural 1 still botches        |

**Armor and Damage**

- **Total the damage first.** Burst and Full Auto arrive as one packet.

- **Then armor answers.** Roll PROT, add RES where the damage type allows. AP skips RES. Enemy armor is static.

- **What’s left** comes off Health Levels, left to right.

- **Withering** — heals only with rest and medicine, and not until you're clear of the source. Armor works as normal.

- **Massive** — skips all of the above. Strips Integrity equal to the weapon's damage and takes 1 Health Level per 10 points of it, plus another if the armor drops to 0 or there was none. Those Levels don't come back with rest.

- **Integrity** — 1 point for every hit the armor stops outright. Anyone hit at all rolls once for wear at the end of the encounter, 1d4 to 1d10, depending on difficulty.

- **At Integrity 0** — RES gone, PROT remains. Armor taken to 0 by Massive is scrap.
